paragraphs: Two neural networks can implement the same function even when their parameters look different. This matters for model fusion: combining parameters is easier when equivalent internal representations are aligned. The paper studies how to obtain that alignment in transformers by exploiting transformations that preserve a model’s function.

The authors introduce rotation symmetry in self-attention layers. Permutation symmetry rearranges parameter coordinates, whereas rotation symmetry allows continuous transformations of parameter matrices. This expands the set of equivalent transformer representations available for matching. The practical significance is that alignment can search beyond discrete rearrangements when bringing separately trained models into correspondence.

Using this symmetry, the authors develop a parameter matching algorithm described as theoretically optimal, packaged as a module for model fusion. Experiments with pretrained transformers on language and vision tasks report substantial improvements in fusion. These findings support continuous symmetry as a useful resource for matching models; the optimality claim concerns parameter matching, while the benefits to fusion are established experimentally.
icml-2025-beyond-the-permutation-symmetr.tldr: Rotation symmetry expands the ways transformer parameters can be aligned, enabling a matching algorithm that improves model fusion in language and vision experiments.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual patterns in events that occur over continuous time requires more than a sensitive anomaly score. A detector also needs control over how often it flags normal sequences. This paper introduces CADES, a conformal testing procedure that combines anomaly detection with finite-sample guarantees on the false positive rate.

CADES uses the time-rescaling theorem to construct two non-conformity scores, which measure departures from expected event behavior. The scores respond to different kinds of abnormalities, making their sensitivities complementary. The method combines them using Bonferroni correction, so using multiple signals is incorporated into the false positive control. It also addresses non-identifiability issues in existing approaches.

The authors prove the procedure’s validity and provide additional guarantees concerning false positive control conditional on calibration data. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets cover several anomaly types and report better performance than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining false positive control. The contribution therefore connects detection quality with statistical reliability, rather than assessing success solely through the strength of an anomaly score.
icml-2025-conformal-anomaly-detection-in.tldr: CADES combines complementary event-sequence anomaly scores with conformal inference to improve detection while providing finite-sample false positive control.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using observed context and learn from the rewards those actions produce. This paper studies the nonparametric setting when contexts can extend beyond any bounded region. Such distributions complicate learning because the method must balance action exploration with the accuracy of reward estimates in unevenly sampled parts of the context space.

The authors propose two methods that combine nearest-neighbor estimation with upper confidence bound exploration. One uses a fixed number of neighbors. The other selects that number adaptively from data. Choosing the neighborhood size controls a second tradeoff: using more observations can stabilize estimates, but incorporating less similar contexts can introduce bias.

The fixed-neighborhood method achieves minimax optimal regret under a weak margin condition and relatively light-tailed context distributions. The adaptive method has an expected regret bound depending on context dimension, the margin parameter, and tail strength. Its bound matches a minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors. This establishes approximate optimality within the analyzed setting and clarifies how unbounded context distributions affect achievable learning performance.
icml-2025-contextual-bandits-for-unbound.tldr: Nearest-neighbor bandit methods with confidence-based exploration achieve qualified optimality guarantees for context distributions with unbounded support.

paragraphs: Learning systems for circuit design often target individual tasks, requiring specialized datasets and leaving representations isolated across applications. DeepLayout instead develops a general representation framework for backend circuit design. Its focus is on placed circuits, where understanding a layout requires both its connectivity structure and the physical arrangement of its components.

The encoder combines a graph neural network with spatial transformers to capture these two forms of information. A flexible decoder supports different tasks and output levels, including nets and complete layouts. This architecture gives the framework a way to reuse circuit representations while adapting its outputs to the particular assessment being performed.

To address annotation costs, the authors introduce layout-specific masked self-supervised learning with reconstruction guidance, alongside two supervised learning tasks. Experiments on large industrial datasets show performance above state-of-the-art task-specific methods on two layout quality assessment benchmarks. The results support the value of learning shared circuit properties, with the reported evidence centered on those assessment tasks rather than every stage of circuit design.
icml-2025-deeplayout-learning-neural-rep.tldr: DeepLayout combines circuit connectivity and geometry in a reusable representation framework that outperforms specialized methods on two layout assessment benchmarks.

paragraphs: Long sequences make multidimensional transformers expensive in both memory and computation. Sequence parallelism distributes sequence processing, but the existing approaches described in this paper divide work along a single sequence dimension. That fixed choice can require substantial communication even when different computation stages expose independent work along different dimensions.

Dynamic Sequence Parallelism, or DSP, changes the dimension used to distribute work as computation proceeds. An efficient resharding strategy rearranges the distribution between stages. The central idea is to make the parallel layout follow the structure of the current calculation, taking advantage of the multiple sequence dimensions already present in these transformers.

The authors describe DSP as adaptable across modules and implementable with few constraints. In their evaluations, it improves throughput by amounts ranging from 32.2% to tenfold compared with state-of-the-art embedded sequence parallelism methods, while using less than one quarter of their communication volume. These experimental results show how changing work distribution can improve execution efficiency without requiring a single parallel dimension to serve every stage.
icml-2025-dsp-dynamic-sequence-paralleli.tldr: DSP switches the sequence dimension used for parallel computation across stages, reducing communication and substantially improving measured transformer throughput.

paragraphs: Visual tracking follows a target through video, but the paper argues that many trackers rely mainly on appearance and underuse motion continuity. Processing temporal information is difficult, so useful evidence about the target’s trajectory can be left out. The authors propose a lightweight motion module that can be added to existing vision-based trackers.

A motion encoder represents the target’s long-term trajectory using three positional encodings and maps it into the visual embedding space. This makes motion information available in a form that can interact with visual features. A fusion decoder and adaptive weighting mechanism then combine the two information sources dynamically during tracking.

The module is integrated into three trackers, covering five models, and evaluated on seven challenging benchmarks. The experiments report significant robustness improvements with minimal training costs and negligible loss of speed. The results support adding temporal evidence through a small, reusable component: the existing tracker supplies visual discrimination, while the motion prompt contributes information about how the target has moved over time.
icml-2025-efficient-motion-prompt-learni.tldr: A lightweight motion prompt module improves existing visual trackers by adaptively combining long-term trajectory information with appearance features.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery seeks varied, distinguishable behaviors without starting from a prescribed task reward. Existing approaches can explore effectively yet become inefficient, especially in high-dimensional settings. This paper asks how skill generation can focus on behaviors for which the learning policy still has meaningful room to improve.

The authors formulate skill generation and policy learning as a min-max game built on temporal representation learning. A regret-based score measures how far a skill’s strength is from convergence. A learnable generator uses that signal to direct more exploration toward weak skills and less toward skills whose strength has converged. An upgradable population of generators is introduced to avoid degeneration of skill generation.

Experiments across environments with different complexities and dimensions report improvements over baselines in both efficiency and skill diversity. The authors also report a 15% zero-shot improvement in high-dimensional environments. These findings support directing exploration according to remaining learning opportunity, so the expanding skill space stays connected to capabilities the policy can still develop.
icml-2025-efficient-skill-discovery-via-.tldr: Regret-guided skill generation concentrates exploration where policies can still improve, yielding more efficient and diverse skill discovery in experiments.

paragraphs: Graph pooling builds broader representations by grouping nodes and combining their information. The challenge is preserving meaningful structure as the graph becomes more compact. ENAHPool addresses two problems identified in existing cluster-based methods: unclear node assignments and aggregation that treats edge and node information uniformly instead of weighting their contributions.

The proposed pooling operation assigns each node to exactly one cluster. Attention then weights node features inside each cluster and connection strengths between clusters. This allows the hierarchy to represent both what a group contains and how groups relate to one another, with different contributions receiving different weights during aggregation.

The paper also introduces a Multi-Distance Message Passing Neural Network that uses connection strengths to transmit information directly and selectively across multiple distances. This is designed to mitigate over-squashing, the difficulty of compressing extensive incoming information through message passing. Experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. Together, the components address how graph information is summarized and how it travels, supporting more informative hierarchical graph representations.
icml-2025-enahpool-the-edge-node-attenti.tldr: ENAHPool combines exclusive graph clustering with attention-weighted aggregation, alongside selective multi-distance message passing to improve graph representations.

paragraphs: Federated Q-learning allows multiple agents to contribute to learning action values, but both learning mistakes and communication incur costs. This paper analyzes those costs for on-policy learning in tabular, episodic, finite-horizon decision processes. Its key assumption is a strictly positive suboptimality gap, separating inferior actions from optimal choices.

That favorable structure permits a logarithmic-in-time regret bound instead of the square-root-in-time bounds associated with worst-case analyses. Here, time refers to the average number of interaction steps per agent. The analysis also identifies a distinct pattern of multi-agent speedup, showing that exploiting the gap changes how the benefit of additional agents appears in the guarantee.

The communication analysis separates exploration from exploitation and removes dependence on the product of agent, state, and action counts from the logarithmic time term. This does not remove those quantities from every possible cost term. For a single agent, the same result improves the global switching-cost bound by removing the state-action factor from its logarithmic time term.
icml-2025-gap-dependent-bounds-for-feder.tldr: A positive suboptimality gap enables logarithmic regret and sharper communication guarantees for federated Q-learning in finite-horizon tabular settings.

paragraphs: Multi-camera 3D object detectors need to work beyond the conditions represented in their training data. Collecting and labeling many different domains is expensive, so this paper studies generalization when training data comes from only one source. The goal is to improve performance on other domains without requiring a collection of diverse training sources.

The proposed Fourier Cross-View Learning framework has two components. Fourier Hierarchical Augmentation modifies data in the frequency domain to increase training diversity. A cross-view semantic consistency loss encourages the detector to learn features that remain meaningful across neighboring camera perspectives and are less tied to a particular domain.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees using augmentation graph theory and evaluate the framework across multiple testing domains. Their experiments report the best performance among the domain generalization methods compared. The approach connects two sources of training information: variation created through augmentation and semantic agreement across camera views. The results support this combination as a way to improve generalization under the stated single-source training constraint.
icml-2025-generalizable-multi-camera-3d-.tldr: Fourier augmentation and cross-view consistency improve multi-camera 3D detection across testing domains when training uses only one source.

paragraphs: Safety training can leave language models vulnerable to prompts that induce harmful responses. This paper examines direct preference optimization, or DPO, and identifies limitations in its suitability for learning refusals through both experiments and gradient analysis. The authors use those findings to redesign the safety objective around two distinct training goals.

One goal strengthens refusal behavior even after a partial unsafe continuation has already been produced. The other targets unlearning of harmful knowledge. Separating these objectives lets training address both the ability to refuse and the harmful information being suppressed. A further reward-based weighting mechanism emphasizes individual tokens that are especially important for learning refusal.

The approach substantially improves robustness against prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations. Token weighting provides further gains. The study also suggests correlations between robustness, changes in token distributions during training, and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens. Those associations offer research directions, while the reported robustness improvements concern the attacks and settings evaluated.
icml-2025-improving-llm-safety-alignment.tldr: Separating robust refusal training from harmful-knowledge unlearning, with extra weight on critical refusal tokens, improves resistance to evaluated jailbreak attacks.

paragraphs: Generative models that learn through denoising typically cannot be applied directly when clean training observations are unavailable. This creates a problem for scientific applications where the desired clean signal is precisely what cannot be measured. Inverse Flow provides a framework for bringing these models to inverse generation tasks, including denoising without ground truth.

The framework accommodates nearly any continuous noise distribution and permits complex dependencies. The authors introduce two learning algorithms: Inverse Flow Matching and an Inverse Consistency Model. To obtain a computationally efficient, simulation-free objective for the latter, they generalize consistency training to arbitrary forward diffusion processes or conditional flows, giving that development relevance beyond denoising alone.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show improvements over previous approaches while supporting noise distributions those methods cannot handle. Applications include fluorescence microscopy and single-cell genomics. The findings point to two complementary benefits: better results in the reported evaluations and wider applicability when the noise structure falls outside what earlier inverse-generation approaches support.
icml-2025-inverse-flow-and-consistency-m.tldr: Inverse Flow extends generative modeling to denoising without clean observations, supporting broad continuous noise distributions and demonstrating gains on scientific data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how two players can learn approximate Nash equilibrium strategies in zero-sum games with hidden information and sequential decisions. Feedback is limited to rewards for the information-set and action pairs actually experienced in each episode. The learner therefore cannot directly inspect the outcomes of all alternatives when updating its strategy.

The algorithm combines entropy regularization with a specially designed virtual transition over information-set and action pairs. That virtual transition weights a negentropy regularizer and supports efficient approximate policy updates. The construction is used to establish convergence of the latest policy profile itself, giving a guarantee about the strategies currently produced by learning.

The authors prove a finite-time last-iterate convergence rate of approximately k to the power of negative one eighth, with logarithmic factors suppressed, where k counts episodes. The guarantee applies under the stated bandit feedback setting. Experiments on several imperfect-information games show competitive performance against baselines. The main contribution is a quantitative convergence guarantee under restricted feedback, supplemented by empirical evidence of practical competitiveness.
icml-2025-learning-imperfect-information.tldr: An entropy-regularized algorithm provides finite-time convergence of current strategies toward Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games with bandit feedback.

paragraphs: Changing the number of agents can adjust the difficulty of a multi-agent reinforcement learning task. However, automatically selecting that number from episode rewards can be misleading. Rewards may vary substantially, and adding agents may increase total returns even while making it harder to determine which agents deserve credit for an outcome.

The proposed curriculum instead uses a learning-progress measure based on temporal-difference error. It maintains a distribution over agent counts and gradually moves from an initial context distribution toward the distribution required by the final task. This lets curriculum decisions reflect learning progress rather than absolute performance, which may rise simply because more agents participate.

The authors explain that aggregating returns in the progress measure also alleviates the high variance problem. Across three challenging sparse-reward benchmarks, the method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. These findings support choosing training conditions according to how learning is advancing, while explicitly accounting for a feature of multi-agent tasks: changing team size can alter both the reward scale and the difficulty of learning.
icml-2025-learning-progress-driven-multi.tldr: A curriculum guided by temporal-difference learning progress adapts agent counts and improves results on three sparse-reward multi-agent benchmarks.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models sometimes describe objects that are absent from an image. Existing remedies can require curated training data, fine-tuning, or access to a proprietary language model for correcting responses. MARINE addresses the problem during inference by supplying object-level evidence extracted from the image without requiring training or API access.

The framework uses open-source vision models to identify object information and guide the language model’s generation. It can incorporate multiple vision models, allowing their outputs to contribute to more reliable guidance. Its central mechanism is to strengthen the connection between generated descriptions and visual evidence about which objects are actually present.

Evaluations across five vision-language models, multiple benchmarks, and different metrics demonstrate reduced object hallucination, including results above existing fine-tuning methods. In GPT-4V-assisted evaluation, the reductions are consistent while descriptions retain their level of detail. GPT-4V serves in that evaluation, whereas the proposed framework itself is API-free. The findings support adding visual guidance at inference as an effective way to improve grounded descriptions.
icml-2025-mitigating-object-hallucinatio.tldr: MARINE uses open-source vision models to guide image descriptions at inference, reducing object hallucination without training or API access.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models connect visual observations and language to robot decisions, often learning by imitating recorded behavior. Their performance can be constrained when demonstrations vary in quality. ReinboT introduces an end-to-end model that incorporates the reinforcement learning objective of maximizing cumulative reward to make better use of mixed-quality training data.

The model predicts dense returns that capture differences in manipulation behavior and its expected future benefits. These predictions provide a way to represent the quality distribution within the data and guide action generation toward more rewarding outcomes. This connects the model’s understanding of observations and instructions with an explicit assessment of the consequences of its decisions.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN mixed-quality dataset, along with superior few-shot learning and out-of-distribution generalization in real-world tasks. The results support incorporating reward-oriented learning into vision-language-action modeling. In particular, they show the value of distinguishing behavior by its anticipated return when the available examples contain a mixture of stronger and weaker robot performance.
icml-2025-reinbot-amplifying-robot-visua.tldr: ReinboT uses dense return prediction to bring reward-maximizing learning into a vision-language-action model, improving robot performance with mixed-quality data.

paragraphs: Generating a video beyond a model’s usual length can introduce repeated temporal patterns or unnaturally slow motion. This paper investigates those problems through the frequency components of positional embeddings, which provide information about positions in the sequence. The authors identify an intrinsic frequency that primarily governs the model’s behavior when extending video length.

RIFLEx reduces that intrinsic frequency to suppress repetition while maintaining motion consistency. The intervention is deliberately small and requires no additional modifications. Its significance is the connection between a specific part of the positional representation and the temporal failures observed during extrapolation, providing a targeted way to change long-video behavior.

The authors report high-quality generation at twice the original length on state-of-the-art video diffusion transformers without training. With minimal fine-tuning, the approach improves quality and supports threefold extrapolation without using long videos for that fine-tuning. These are two distinct operating conditions: the twofold result is training-free, while the threefold result uses additional learning. Both support the usefulness of adjusting the identified frequency.
icml-2025-riflex-a-free-lunch-for-length.tldr: RIFLEx adjusts an intrinsic positional frequency to enable training-free twofold video-length extrapolation and threefold extrapolation with minimal fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may receive conflicting information from different input modalities. This paper investigates how those conflicts can lead to hallucinations. Its focus is on inconsistency already present within the inputs, creating a dilemma for the model before it produces a response, rather than only on discrepancies between a response and its evidence.

The authors formally define modality conflict and construct the Multimodal Modality Conflict dataset to simulate it in vision-language tasks. They then propose three ways to reduce the resulting hallucinations: prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Evaluating these approaches on a shared dataset allows the study to examine their respective strengths and weaknesses.

Reinforcement learning performs best at mitigating hallucinations under modality conflict in the reported experiments. Supervised fine-tuning also delivers promising, stable performance. These findings identify input disagreement as a useful target for robustness research and provide comparative evidence about ways to address it. The ranking concerns the conflict setting evaluated on this dataset, rather than establishing one method as best for every source of hallucination.
icml-2025-robust-multimodal-large-langua.tldr: A new dataset and three mitigation approaches expose modality conflict as a hallucination source, with reinforcement learning performing best in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Sampling-based search spends inference time generating several candidate answers and checking which one is best. This paper studies how that strategy scales when both generation and verification use simple mechanisms. Even random sampling combined with direct self-verification produces sustained gains as computation increases, including reported benchmark results where Gemini v1.5 Pro surpasses o1-Preview.

The authors partly explain these gains through implicit scaling: a larger response pool can also improve verification accuracy. Comparing answers supplies clues about where errors or hallucinations occur. They also find that the best output style depends on the task being performed; chains of thought help reasoning but are harder to verify.

The study nevertheless finds that frontier models have weak verification capabilities out of the box, even though stronger checking can be elicited. It introduces a benchmark to measure progress on those deficiencies. Together, the findings emphasize verification as an active part of inference-time scaling: generating additional candidates can provide more material for comparison, but effective checking still requires attention to how it is elicited.
icml-2025-sample-scrutinize-and-scale-ef.tldr: Scaling simple sampling and self-verification improves reasoning, partly because larger candidate pools provide better signals for checking answers.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning diffusion models with reward feedback aims to make their generated outputs better match prompts. Many approaches formulate this process in discrete time, which can introduce errors and often does not accommodate higher-order or black-box solvers. This paper develops a continuous-time reinforcement learning formulation for the fine-tuning problem.

The authors express generation as stochastic control, with a reward assessing how well the final output aligns with the prompt. The key move is to treat score matching as the control or action, connecting the diffusion model’s learned behavior to policy optimization and regularization. This creates a framework for optimizing the generative process in continuous time.

The work also explores how diffusion structure can inform the design of value networks within this policy optimization framework. Experiments on downstream fine-tuning tasks using Stable Diffusion v1.5 validate advantages of the method. Its contribution combines a disciplined mathematical formulation with an empirical application, showing how the continuous-time view can guide both optimization and the supporting networks used to evaluate future reward.
icml-2025-score-as-action-fine-tuning-di.tldr: Treating diffusion scores as control actions enables a continuous-time reinforcement learning framework for reward-guided fine-tuning of text-to-image models.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while retaining information about where cells are located. Understanding these data requires linking several scales: the overall tissue structure, a cell’s local surroundings, and its gene expression profile. SToFM is a foundation model designed to combine those scales when learning representations of cells within tissue slices.

The framework first extracts information at multiple scales and constructs smaller spatial transcriptomics sub-slices that bring the three kinds of evidence together. An SE(2) Transformer then processes these sub-slices to produce cell representations. The authors also build SToCorpus-88M, described as the largest high-resolution spatial transcriptomics pretraining corpus, to support learning from this type of data.

The model achieves strong reported performance across downstream tasks, including tissue region segmentation and cell type annotation. These tasks use the learned representations at different biological levels, connecting cell identity with tissue organization. The results support integrating spatial context and gene expression in a shared model, showing that the combined information can be useful across multiple forms of spatial transcriptomics analysis.
icml-2025-stofm-a-multi-scale-foundation.tldr: SToFM integrates tissue structure, cellular surroundings, and gene expression to learn cell representations that perform strongly across spatial transcriptomics tasks.

paragraphs: Cell instance segmentation must distinguish individual cells, including cells pressed tightly against one another. This paper changes how that distinction is represented. Inspired by the four-color theorem, it treats cells like regions on a map and assigns adjacent cells different labels using an encoding with only four classes.

The encoding turns instance segmentation into a constrained semantic segmentation problem. The model predicts a small set of reusable classes while the adjacency constraint preserves distinctions between touching instances. This simplifies the labeling problem, but introduces an ambiguity: the same arrangement of cells can have multiple valid four-color encodings, creating instability during training.

The authors address that non-uniqueness with an asymptotic training strategy and an encoding transformation method. Extensive experiments across different modes report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is therefore both a reformulation and a way to train it effectively. A compact class vocabulary becomes useful for separating many instances because the encoding imposes local relationships between neighboring cells, rather than requiring every cell to have its own predicted class.
icml-2025-the-four-color-theorem-for-cel.tldr: A four-color encoding separates adjacent cells through constrained semantic segmentation, with specialized training to handle multiple valid encodings.

paragraphs: Converting a pretrained artificial neural network into a spiking network offers a way to use existing learned parameters without retraining. Time-to-first-spike coding is particularly attractive for energy efficiency because each neuron emits at most one spike. However, applying this coding to transformers is difficult because attention and nonlinear layers require representations that existing approaches struggle to provide.

TTFSFormer introduces a neuron structure that expands the representational range of time-to-first-spike coding and improves its ability to process nonlinear functions. The paper also provides nonlinear neuron designs tailored to different transformer layers. These components address the operations that make transformer conversion more challenging than earlier applications of the coding scheme to convolutional networks.

Experiments across different models show high accuracy with significantly lower energy consumption. The authors describe the work as the first focused on transformer-to-spiking conversion using time-to-first-spike coding. The reported findings connect architectural changes at the neuron level with the broader goal of efficient transformer execution, extending a low-spike coding approach to attention-based models.
icml-2025-ttfsformer-a-ttfs-based-lossle.tldr: TTFSFormer introduces neuron designs that support transformer conversion to time-to-first-spike networks with high accuracy and lower measured energy consumption.

paragraphs: Different neural network minima can often be connected by parameter-space curves along which training and test losses change little. This phenomenon, called mode connectivity, is useful for merging and fine-tuning models, but its theoretical explanation remains incomplete. The paper investigates it through parameter symmetries: transformations that relate equivalent network representations.

The authors connect the topology of symmetry groups with the topology of network minima. For linear networks, they derive the number of connected components and show that skip connections reduce that number. They also examine conditions under which curved-path connectivity and straight-line connectivity hold or fail, using symmetries that account for a significant portion of the minimum.

The work gives explicit formulas for connecting curves within minima that arise from symmetry. Analyzing their curvature then yields conditions under which straight-line connections approximately preserve the relevant low-loss behavior. These results provide a geometric explanation for part of the observed connectivity, highlighting continuous symmetries while keeping the linear-network results and conditional statements distinct from universal claims about all neural networks.
icml-2025-understanding-mode-connectivit.tldr: Parameter-space symmetries explain aspects of connected neural network minima and yield conditions for approximate straight-line connectivity.

paragraphs: Dataset inference investigates whether a collection of data was used to train a model. Existing methods require comparison data that matches the suspected dataset’s distribution but is known to have been excluded from training. Such a private held-out collection is often unavailable, limiting the ability to investigate training-data use after the fact.

The authors replace that missing comparison collection with synthetic data. A generator trained on a specially designed suffix-completion task produces diverse text intended to reflect the original distribution. Post-hoc calibration then addresses likelihood differences between real and generated examples. Both components matter: matching the content distribution alone does not resolve the scoring gap between synthetic and real data.

Across diverse text datasets, experiments show that the generated comparison sets enable high-confidence detection of original training datasets while maintaining a low false positive rate. The findings support a more practical route to post-hoc dataset inference when suitable held-out data was never reserved. The authors position this capability as evidence that could help data owners substantiate claims about unauthorized training use.
icml-2025-unlocking-post-hoc-dataset-inf.tldr: Synthetic comparison data and post-hoc calibration enable dataset inference without a preexisting private held-out set, with strong reported detection and low false positives.
